items.title: 9 Classics Where the Audiobook Version Is Better
items.summary: Audiobooks were technically born as far back as 1877, with Thomas Edison 's invention of the phonograph. Andy Muschietti’s long-delayed The Brave and the Bold has been thrown into complete uncertainty, while Matt Reeves’ The Batman sees its prospects for a third installment become increasingly dim. items.title: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping review – surreally awful prequel to the Katniss Everdeen era
items.summary:
Overwrought and boring, this nadir of a prequel to the Games’ death match saga is nothing but a cash grab for an exhausted franchise

Here is yet another iteration of the utterly exhausted, unbearably extended and now surreally boring Hunger Games franchise, based on the YA bestsellers by Suzanne Collins. This one has another of the series’ convoluted faux-mythic subtitles: Sunrise on the Reaping. What, “harvest dawn” not old-timey enough?

Well, “reaping” in fact refers to an annual process by which ordinary smudgy faced, raggedy clothed people are chosen at random for compulsory participation in this futurist dystopia’s brutal, televised survival contest to the death: a bread-and-circuses nightmare with which the rulers keep the populace in a cowed and pacified state. In this Darwinian process, competitors strategically team up with (and then betray) some players against others in the short term, to stay in the game.

items.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
items.summary:
Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary

Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that this physical media holds.

Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic. “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau

items.title: American Doctor review – medics put their lives on the line in Gaza amid the carnage
items.summary:
Poh Si Teng’s powerful documentary follows three doctors from the US who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital

This is the latest documentary about medics travelling to Palestine to treat civilian casualties; it’s a powerful, angry film, in a state of despair at the scale of suffering and devastation. A sliver of hope is the trio of doctors it profiles, individuals acting on their conscience. (The same can be said of director Poh Si Teng, who quit her job at ABC News and cashed in her savings to get the documentary off the ground.) It follows three American doctors who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital in southern Gaza in early 2025 – though one of the trio, Thaer Ahmad, an ER doctor of Palestinian heritage from Chicago, is refused entry the night before they enter Gaza.

His colleagues, Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon, and Dr Mark Perlmutter, a Jewish-American orthopaedic surgeon, complete the mission. This is not the first time in Gaza for either of them. Before he leaves, Perlmutter packs antibiotics into a dozen or so little plastic bags dotted around his luggage; that way if he gets turned back at the border, he stands a chance of getting some of the life-saving medication through. Given the high death rate of medics in the war, he also gets a will drawn up before he goes.

Continue reading...
items.t: American Doctor review – medics put their lives on the line in Gaza amid the carnage

items.title: Rocky is Philadelphia’s founding myth – and 50 years later, we’re still telling it
items.summary:
As Sylvester Stallone’s Oscar-winning drama celebrates its 50th anniversary, I Play Rocky helps to further turn the boxing hero into the stuff of legend

The story behind the making of Rocky has always sounded uncannily like Rocky itself. An unknown with an improbable dream, a skeptical establishment and a refusal to accept the odds: Sylvester Stallone’s real-life struggle to crack the industry and bring his breakthrough film to the screen contained all the elements of the underdog story he sought to tell. Now, half a century later, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky has crafted those parallels into a crowd-pleasing yarn of its own.

It’s an extraordinary afterlife for a modest boxing flick that became the highest-grossing film of 1976 on a $1m budget and won the Oscar for best picture over one of the most stacked fields in history. Yet its greatest achievement may be the durability of the story – dismissed then by the New York Times as a “sentimental little slum movie” and Gene Siskel as a “flatout schmaltzy saga” – that we’re still finding new ways to repurpose all these years later through six Rocky films, three Creed sequels, a Broadway musical, and too many documentaries, novelizations and video games to count. At some point long ago, a screenplay written in three and a half days and never envisioned as IP became something closer to contemporary folklore.
items.t: Rocky is Philadelphia’s founding myth – and 50 years later, we’re still telling it

items.title: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw
items.summary:
Pattinson is a character actor whose talent for inscrutable appraisal may mean a new era for 007. Will this more willowy, classy Bond leave sexism in the shadows?

• New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
• Share your thoughts on the casting
• Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to James Bond

If it wasn’t Bond … maybe it would have been Dr No in some hi-tech reboot. But Robert Pattinson – with his movie-star chops and track record in hip A24-type character turns, and his gift for cool, inscrutable appraisal and sensual menace – is an exquisite choice as 007, playing on the darker and more sophisticated notes of Pattinson’s performing personality.

And let’s hope, incidentally, that the actor now isn’t forced into a five-hour daily gym regimen to bulk up. I like the taller and more willowy Bond that Pattinson represents, the Bond from whose frame the tux hangs gracefully, the Bond with elegant abandon who’s a former British Naval officer, not a former US Navy Seal, the Bond who with a crinkly-eyed reptilian grin can style out waking up with a hangover after too many whisky-and-sodas at the baccarat table.
items.t: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw

items.title: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
items.summary:
The adventurous weirdness of the Gunn/Safran era that fans responded to is now history. Can the DCU ever get back on track?

What was Warner Bros’ plan in 2022, when the studio decided to reboot its superhero output, jettison the increasingly muddled DC Extended Universe (DCEU) and replace it with a sparkling new DC Universe (DCU)? In part it was to wipe the slate clean after years of false starts, abandoned storylines and tonal lurches. There was a little bit of Marvel envy to proceedings, and quite possibly a desire to avoid having to ever again discuss Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice’s numerous failings. But mostly it was to take advantage of hiring of a man whom nobody could accuse of being short of ideas on how to make comic book movies. To a greater or lesser extent, the plan was James Gunn.

Fast forward four years, and that plan lies in tatters. Gunn and his fellow DC Studios CEO Peter Safran have this week been fired (though they will reportedly stay on as film-makers), and Jeremy Latcham, another former Marvel man, is the new boss. What is the plan now? items.title: ‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong
items.summary:
As Amazon MGM Studios prepares to announce the next 007, much rides on how the news is broken. From double bookings to health and safety embarrassments, we look back at how not to do it

And then there were five. While nothing has been officially announced, it is widely understood that the shortlist to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond is now down to a handful of actors: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult.

The hunt for a new Bond comes at a propitious moment for the franchise as a whole, 25 films in (not counting the two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983). After Daniel Craig stood down from the role after completing No Time to Die (in which Bond appeared to be killed in a missile strike), Amazon MGM Studios paid over $1bn to acquire “creative control” from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the British-American heirs to the series’ original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.

items.t: ‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong
